posts.hook: Building your first home? Here’s what actually happens, in order.

cards.label: first home
cards.hook: Building your first home? Here’s what actually happens, in order.
cards.sub: Land contract, build contract, the wait, the progress payments. The order matters more than people think.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Contract order comes first
cards.body: Whether you sign land and build together or land first changes which low-deposit options you qualify for. We work the order out before anyone signs a block.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: The land contract gets reviewed
cards.body: We won’t let a client sign a developer’s land contract without a solicitor reading it. Titling dates, sunset clauses and finance timing all live in there.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Ask for a fixed price
cards.body: Fixed-price and completion-time clauses are harder to get than they were. They are still negotiable at signing. Ask every time. You lose nothing.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Where a build loses time
cards.body: Two places: land titling and the builder. Land delays cost you little, no mortgage has started. Builder delays cost rent and interest together. Put your energy there.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Progress payments, step by step
cards.body: You don’t pay on the whole loan from day one. Money goes to the builder in stages, usually interest-only, so repayments rise as the house does.

cards.label: first home
cards.headline: Building? Get the order right first.
cards.body: Fifteen minutes before you sign anything saves months later.

posts.linkedin:
Building your first home? Here's what actually happens, in order.

Most people start with the builder's brochure. We start with the paperwork order, because whether you sign the land and build contracts together or land first can change which low-deposit options you qualify for. That decision is made before anyone signs a block.

Then the land contract goes to a solicitor, every time. Titling dates, sunset clauses and finance timing live in that document, and a developer's contract is written for the developer.

The slide on where a build loses time is the one to screenshot. Land delays cost you very little. Builder delays cost you rent and interest at the same time. That's where the negotiating energy goes.

The rest is in the carousel, including how progress payments actually work.

General information only, not personal advice.

posts.hook: Settlement day is boring when it goes right. Here’s how we keep it boring.

cards.label: first home
cards.hook: Settlement day is boring when it goes right. Here’s how we keep it boring.
cards.sub: What actually happens between approval and keys, and the small things that break it.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Your deposit stays in trust
cards.body: We prefer the deposit sits in the agent’s trust account until settlement. Releasing it early to the seller removes your protection if the deal falls over.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Funds land before settlement
cards.body: You don’t need every dollar in one account on application day. You need it verifiable and in Australia by settlement, with the transfers timed and documented.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: We read the loan documents
cards.body: The moment the deal goes unconditional we check the lender’s documents against what was approved. Interest-only periods and offsets have a habit of going missing in between.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Nothing new on credit
cards.body: Between approval and settlement, no new card, lease or car loan. A fresh commitment can shrink the capacity you were approved on and reopen a finished file.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: If the date moves
cards.body: Ask once, for the full penalty-free window the contract allows, and check what the delay does to the people on the other side before you ask.

cards.label: first home
cards.headline: Settlement should be the dull bit.
cards.body: Tell us your contract dates and we’ll map the rest.

posts.linkedin:
Settlement day is boring when it goes right. Here's how we keep it boring.

The days between approval and keys are where a good purchase gets messy. Not because anything dramatic happens, but because small things get missed.

The deposit stays in the agent's trust account until settlement, because releasing it early hands your protection to the seller. The loan documents get read by us the moment the deal goes unconditional, because the structure we fought for has a habit of going missing between approval and contract.

And nothing new goes on your credit file until the keys are in your hand. A car loan in that window can reopen a file that was finished.

The carousel covers the rest, including what to do if a settlement date has to move.

posts.hook: Mum and Dad going guarantor? Here’s what they actually sign.

cards.label: first home
cards.hook: Mum and Dad going guarantor? Here’s what they actually sign.
cards.sub: What a parental guarantor does, what it doesn’t fix, and the appointment nobody books early enough.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: What it actually solves
cards.body: A strong income with little savings is very financeable when a parent offers their property as security. The loan can cover price and costs. The question becomes servicing.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: What it doesn’t fix
cards.body: A guarantor fixes a deposit problem, not a repayment problem. If the shortfall is servicing, the fix is lower monthly commitments, not Mum and Dad.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Their house is tied up
cards.body: The parents’ home is committed for several years. If they sell before the security is released, a cash contribution is usually required. The whole family agrees the timeline.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: The legal advice appointment
cards.body: Guarantors need a certificate of independent legal advice. A JP can’t sign it, only a solicitor can. We book it the day loan documents are issued.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Guarantor, not co-borrower
cards.body: A parent near retirement on the loan itself is help for a few years, not thirty, because lenders assess their income to retirement. Security alone often achieves more.

cards.label: first home
cards.headline: Helping a child into a home?
cards.body: Bring the parents to the first chat. It’s a family decision.

posts.linkedin:
Mum and Dad going guarantor? Here's what they actually sign.

A parental guarantor is one of the most useful tools we have for a first-home buyer with a strong income and a thin deposit. It is also one of the most misunderstood, usually by the parents.

The slide to start with is what it doesn't fix. A guarantor solves a deposit problem. If the shortfall is in repayments, the parents' signature changes nothing, and the fix is on the monthly commitments instead.

Then the practical bits. Their home is tied up for several years and selling early usually means a cash contribution. And the independent legal advice certificate needs a solicitor, not a JP, which is why we book that appointment the day loan documents are issued rather than discovering it at settlement.

The carousel has all five.

General information only, not personal advice.
posts.instagram:
Mum and Dad going guarantor? Swipe for what they actually sign.

It solves a deposit problem, not a repayment problem. Their home is tied up for several years, and selling early usually means putting cash in. The legal advice certificate needs a solicitor, not a JP. And security from a parent often does more, for longer, than putting a parent near retirement on the loan itself.

Has your family talked about the release timeline, or just the signature?

posts.hook: What actually happens when you ask us to refinance. Sometimes we say don’t.

cards.label: refinancing
cards.hook: What actually happens when you ask us to refinance. Sometimes we say don’t.
cards.sub: Valuation first, paperwork second, and a few honest reasons to leave a good loan alone.

cards.label: refinancing
cards.title: Sometimes the answer is no
cards.body: We won’t move a loan just to move it. If you already have a good rate and we can’t add a real structural benefit, we’d rather leave it alone.

cards.label: refinancing
cards.title: Valuation before payslips
cards.body: Before we ask for a single document we order valuations, because the property value decides whether a refinance is even worth doing.

cards.label: refinancing
cards.title: One valuation is one opinion
cards.body: The spread between lenders’ valuations can be the difference between a yes and a no. We run several before committing anywhere.

cards.label: refinancing
cards.title: Repricing can beat moving
cards.body: If a valuation lands you close to the next pricing tier, a modest lump sum and a reprice with your current lender can beat discharging. Same offsets, no exit fees.

cards.label: refinancing
cards.title: Moving is one form
cards.body: Switching banks is redirecting your salary into the new offset. Bills can stay where they are. And the new loan settles slightly above the payout on purpose; the surplus lands in your offset.

cards.label: refinancing
cards.headline: Not sure your loan needs moving?
cards.body: Ask us. The honest answer might be leave it.

posts.linkedin:
What actually happens when you ask us to refinance. Sometimes we say don't.

We won't move a loan just to move it. If you already have a good rate and we can't add a real structural benefit, a needed cash-out, a cleaner split, a better fit for the next purchase, we'd rather leave it alone and tell you so.

When it is worth looking at, the order matters. Valuation first, paperwork second. The property value decides whether the exercise makes sense, so we order valuations with several lenders before asking for a payslip.

The slide on repricing is the quiet one. Sometimes a small lump sum and a reprice with your current bank does more than a move, with no exit fees and the same offsets.

The rest, including why the new loan settles slightly above the old balance, is in the carousel.

posts.hook: Funding your business from your home’s equity. What actually happens.

cards.label: business owners
cards.hook: Funding your business from your home’s equity. What actually happens.
cards.sub: The cheapest money, the house question, the separate pocket, and the paperwork your accountant will want.

cards.label: business owners
cards.title: Why it’s the cheapest money
cards.body: Credit secured by residential property is usually the cheapest funding a business can get, compared with an unsecured line or overdraft. That’s why the question comes up.

cards.label: business owners
cards.title: Is the house in?
cards.body: We start unsecured or with the smallest security a lender accepts. If property has to come in, an investment property goes before the family home. Your call, and we respect it.

cards.label: business owners
cards.title: A pocket, not a top-up
cards.body: Business funds sit in their own interest-only split beside the home loan. The pocket carries its own purpose; the home loan keeps getting paid down untouched.

cards.label: business owners
cards.title: Draw from the offset
cards.body: Funds are drawn into an offset, never transacted through redraw. The money costs nothing until used and the loan stays clean for your accountant.

cards.label: business owners
cards.title: Paper the entity loan
cards.body: If you borrow personally and lend to your company or trust, ask your accountant whether a formal loan agreement is needed before the funds move. Usually yes.

cards.label: business owners
cards.headline: Business needs cash? Start with the structure.
cards.body: One conversation with your broker and accountant before the bank.

posts.linkedin:
Funding your business from your home's equity. What actually happens.

It comes up because the maths is hard to argue with. Credit secured by residential property is usually the cheapest money a business can borrow.

But the next slide is the one we spend the most time on: do you want the house involved at all? We start unsecured or with the smallest security a lender will take. If property has to come in, an investment property goes before anyone's family home. Plenty of owners say no, and we respect that.

If you proceed, the structure is a separate interest-only pocket beside the home loan, drawn through an offset, never redraw, with a loan agreement to the entity if your accountant says so.

And one voice talks to the bank. Two requests to one lender at once is how both die.

General information only, not personal advice.

posts.hook: Before you sign a land or off-the-plan contract, five checks.

cards.label: first home
cards.hook: Before you sign a land or off-the-plan contract, five checks.
cards.sub: The developer’s contract is written for the developer. Here’s what we look for before you sign.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: A lawyer has read it
cards.body: We don’t let a client sign a developer’s contract without a solicitor reviewing it first. If you don’t have one, we refer one.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: The sunset clause
cards.body: Developers use sunset clauses to buy themselves time. Negotiate it at signing, and never sign an extension request without your solicitor and broker seeing what it does to your finance.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Land plus build vs established
cards.body: Add up land and build, then look at what finished homes nearby sell for. If the new build is well above, it has to justify the gap on quality, not newness.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: A finance clause
cards.body: A lender won’t put an unusual property in writing before a valuation, and the valuation needs a signed contract. The finance clause is how you sign and still have an exit.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: The grant is a bonus
cards.body: We plan settlement as if any grant might not land in time. Keep enough of your own cash to settle without it, and chase it afterwards.

cards.label: first home
cards.headline: Got a contract in your inbox?
cards.body: Send it to us before you send it back.

posts.linkedin:
Before you sign a land or off-the-plan contract, five checks.

A developer's contract is written by the developer's lawyers for the developer's benefit. That's not sinister, it's just who drafted it. So the first rule is simple: a solicitor reads it before you sign, and if you don't have one, we refer one.

The sunset clause slide is the one people skip and regret. It can be negotiated at signing, and when the developer runs late and asks you to extend, that request goes to your solicitor and broker before anyone replies.

And the finance clause. A lender won't commit to an unusual property in writing before a valuation, and the valuation needs a signed contract. The clause is how you sign and still have a penalty-free way out.

The other two are in the carousel.

General information only, not personal advice.

A solicitor reads it first. The sunset clause gets negotiated at signing and never extended without advice. Land plus build gets compared to established homes nearby. There's a finance clause so you can sign and still have an exit. And the grant is a bonus, never the deposit.

posts.hook: Before you sign the loan documents, five things to check.

cards.label: money habits
cards.hook: Before you sign the loan documents, five things to check.
cards.sub: Approved isn’t the same as written down. Here’s what we read before the documents reach you.

cards.label: money habits
cards.title: Does it match the approval?
cards.body: Repayment type, term, offset, interest-only period. The structure we fought for has a habit of going missing between approval and contract. Check every line.

cards.label: money habits
cards.title: Fees: the worst-case list
cards.body: The documents list every fee the lender could ever charge, because the law says so. Most never apply. Ask which two or three you will actually pay.

cards.label: money habits
cards.title: Enough offset accounts
cards.body: On a joint loan we set up one offset per partner, so each keeps their own savings visible and working against the same debt. Ask now, not after.

cards.label: money habits
cards.title: The longest term available
cards.body: Write it over thirty years and pay it like twenty-five. The long term protects your capacity for the next move. Your extra repayments do the real work.

cards.label: money habits
cards.title: The napkin test
cards.body: If the structure can’t be drawn on one page with arrows showing where money flows, it is too complicated to run. Ask for the drawing before you sign.

cards.label: money habits
cards.headline: Documents arrived and look like a phone book?
cards.body: Send them over. We’ll walk the pages that matter.

posts.linkedin:
Before you sign the loan documents, five things to check.

Approved isn't the same as written down. We read the loan documents on the lender portal the moment a deal goes unconditional, before they reach the client, because the structure we fought for has a habit of going missing between approval and contract. Interest-only periods especially.

The fee schedule slide is there to calm you down. The documents list every fee the lender could ever charge because the law requires it. Most are for situations you'll never meet. Ask which two or three you will actually pay.

And the napkin test. If your structure can't be drawn on one page with arrows showing where the money moves, it's too clever to run correctly. We'd rather draw it for you now than explain it later.

All five in the carousel.

General information only, not personal advice.

posts.hook: Buying with a sibling or a mate? Settle these five things first.

cards.label: first home
cards.hook: Buying with a sibling or a mate? Settle these five things first.
cards.sub: Two names on a title is simple. Two names on a loan, years later, is where it gets interesting.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: The next lender’s view
cards.body: When one of you later wants to buy alone, some lenders count only your share of the joint loan. Others count all of it. We model both before anyone co-buys.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: One lives there, one invests
cards.body: The loan can be split: an owner-occupier portion for the resident, an investment portion for the other. It takes workshopping, but it is a normal structure.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Title versus loan
cards.body: If someone is on the title but not the loan, most lenders still want them as a guarantor or co-borrower. Decide who is on what with your solicitor before you apply.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Nothing moves without both
cards.body: Any refinance or restructure against a jointly owned property needs both owners to agree. Have the conversation together before you come to us.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Security isn’t servicing
cards.body: A co-owner can sign as a security guarantor so you can borrow against the property without their income being assessed. Most people only need that.

cards.label: first home
cards.headline: Co-buying? Draw it up before you sign.
cards.body: A short chat now is cheaper than a disagreement later.

posts.linkedin:
Buying with a sibling or a mate? Settle these five things first.

Co-buying gets people into the market who couldn't do it alone. It also creates a loan that follows both of you for years, so we have the awkward conversations now.

The first slide decides whether it's a good idea. When one of you later wants to buy alone, some lenders count only your share of the joint loan against you. Others count the whole thing. We model it both ways before advising anyone to co-buy.

If one of you will live there and the other won't, the loan can be split into an owner-occupier portion and an investment portion. It takes workshopping with lenders, but it's a normal structure and nobody has to pretend anything.

Title versus loan, both signatures, and the security-only option are in the carousel.

General information only, not personal advice.

posts.hook: Before you sign a fixed-price build contract, five things.

cards.label: first home
cards.hook: Before you sign a fixed-price build contract, five things.
cards.sub: The price you lock is the price you pay. Here’s what we check before you lock it.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Lock the price early
cards.body: Build prices move while you wait. Once the land is certain, lock a fixed-price contract and read the terms. Builders are changing them.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Two more quotes anyway
cards.body: Even if you’ve signed a preliminary agreement, send your final spec to two other builders. Differences can be large, and the quotes confirm you’re paying market rate.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: The builder, not the newness
cards.body: A new home is only as new as the builder who built it. Ask for addresses of homes they finished five years ago and go and look.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Compare them side by side
cards.body: A display village puts several builders next to each other. You compare inclusions, quality and price in an afternoon, not one a weekend.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Pay for the inspecting lender
cards.body: Some lenders charge a construction fee because they send a valuer to check each stage before releasing money. We recommend that over fee-free. It’s a second set of eyes.

cards.label: first home
cards.headline: About to sign with a builder?
cards.body: Send us the contract and the quote. Fifteen minutes.

posts.linkedin:
Before you sign a fixed-price build contract, five things.

The price you lock today is the price you pay, which is exactly why we want it locked early, once the land is certain, and why we want the terms read properly. Builders are changing them.

The slide people push back on is two more quotes. Even if you've already signed a preliminary agreement and intend to stay, send your final spec to two other builders. Price differences can be large, and if you stay put, the quotes confirm you're paying market rate.

Then the question that matters more than the brochure: who is the builder? A new home is only as new as whoever built it. Ask for addresses of houses they finished five years ago and drive past.

The construction fee slide surprises people. Pay for the bank that inspects each stage.

posts.hook: Five things we check on an apartment before you offer.

cards.label: first home
cards.hook: Five things we check on an apartment before you offer.
cards.sub: There’s always a reason someone is selling. These are the places we look for it.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: The body corporate minutes
cards.body: Problems in apartments are often well hidden in the body corporate. Read the minutes and ask what the last three special levies were for.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: The block itself
cards.body: The type we quietly like: older, smaller blocks, no lift, decent land. Ask why the fees are what they are before you fall for a view.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Days on market
cards.body: If similar apartments sold and this one has sat for months, it is telling you something: price, layout or a defect. Dig before you get excited about a bargain.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Who buys it after you
cards.body: A layout the market dislikes is cheap to buy and hard to sell. Ask who the likely buyer is in a few years and whether this suits them.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Whose inspector it is
cards.body: The agent’s recommended inspector and lawyer work in the agent’s world, not yours. The only people checking the property should be paid by you.

cards.label: first home
cards.headline: Found an apartment you like?
cards.body: Send us the listing before the open. We’ll start digging.

posts.linkedin:
Five things we check on an apartment before you offer.

There's always a reason someone is selling. A tired landlord is fine. A building problem is not, and in apartments that reason usually sits in the body corporate records. We read the minutes and ask what the last three special levies were for.

The slide on days on market is the simplest check and the most skipped. If comparable apartments sold and this one has sat for months, something is wrong with the price, the layout or the building. Find out which before you get excited about a bargain.

And the last one is blunt. If the agent recommended the inspector or the lawyer, they are not yours. The only people checking the property should be paid by you.

The block type we quietly like, and the next-buyer test, are in the carousel.

General information only, not personal advice.

posts.hook: Cash is for the offset. Debt is for the asset.

cards.label: investors
cards.hook: Cash is for the offset. Debt is for the asset.
cards.sub: Why we’d rather you borrow for the investment and keep your own money where you can reach it.

cards.label: investors
cards.title: The house grows either way
cards.body: A property grows the same whether you paid cash or borrowed. So we debt-fund the asset and keep your cash deployed where it keeps working.

cards.label: investors
cards.title: Never swap them
cards.body: Cash goes against your home. Borrowing goes to the investment. Paying the deposit from cash and borrowing later muddies the trail and wastes the deductible position.

cards.label: investors
cards.title: Day one can’t be rewound
cards.body: Pay cash at settlement and borrow against the property two weeks later, and the interest may never be deductible. Unwinding that is hard. Decide the source first.

cards.label: investors
cards.title: Same saving, still reachable
cards.body: A bigger deposit and the same money in an offset save the same interest. The deposit is locked. The offset is available any day you need it.

cards.label: investors
cards.title: Interest saved isn’t taxed
cards.body: Cash in an offset saves interest rather than earning it, so there’s no interest income to declare. That’s why it usually beats a savings account for the same dollars.

cards.label: investors
cards.headline: About to pay cash for an investment?
cards.body: Talk to us and your accountant first. It can’t be rewound.

posts.linkedin:
Cash is for the offset. Debt is for the asset.

When a client has the cash to buy an investment outright, we still prefer to borrow for it. The property grows the same either way, and your cash keeps working somewhere you can reach it.

The slide on day one is the one that can't be undone. How you fund a purchase at settlement is a tax event. Pay cash and borrow against the property a fortnight later, and the interest may never be deductible. We decide the source of funds before the contract, with your accountant.

The offset slides explain the other half. A bigger deposit and the same money in an offset save the same interest, but only one is available on a bad day. And interest you don't pay is never taxed.

The tax treatment is one for your accountant.

posts.linkedin:
Negotiate terms, not price. Five moves that cost you nothing.

Buyers think negotiation is about the number. Mostly it's about certainty. A vendor who knows your deal will settle, on a date that suits them, often takes less than a nervous higher offer.

posts.hook: What a bank will and won’t count when you own the business.

cards.label: business owners
cards.hook: What a bank will and won’t count when you own the business.
cards.sub: Tax-smart pay and bank-smart pay are different things. Here’s how a lender reads you.

cards.label: business owners
cards.title: Taxed income counts
cards.body: Drawings and untaxed distributions suit the accountant. Lenders struggle to use income that hasn’t been taxed. If you want to keep borrowing, pay yourself in a way a bank can read.

cards.label: business owners
cards.title: This year’s growth, sometimes
cards.body: If last year’s return understates where the business is now, recent activity statements and interims can annualise income with the right lender. Growth doesn’t always wait a year.

cards.label: business owners
cards.title: Full return, not notice
cards.body: The notice shows the final number. The return shows the deductions, super contributions and add-backs that lift assessable income. Send both.

cards.label: business owners
cards.title: Years on the tools count
cards.body: One year on your own ABN plus ten as an employee in the same trade can be assessed on that continuity. Bring the old payment summaries.

cards.label: business owners
cards.title: Young business? Lead with you
cards.body: A young business is the bank’s hurdle. We lead with the directors’ track record, signed contracts and the growth story, and stack funding if one bank won’t move.

cards.label: business owners
cards.headline: Business owner buying in the next year?
cards.body: Bring your broker and accountant together before the next return.

posts.linkedin:
What a bank will and won't count when you own the business.

Your accountant's job is to make your tax bill small. A lender's job is to find income it can rely on. Those goals pull in opposite directions, and most owners find out mid-application.

The first slide is the hard truth. Drawings and untaxed distributions suit the accountant, but lenders struggle to use income that hasn't been taxed. If you plan to keep borrowing, how you pay yourself has to be readable by a bank. That's a conversation for your broker and accountant together, before the next return.

The slide on growth is the good news. With the right lender, recent activity statements and interims can show this year's income rather than last year's.

Short ABN with years on the tools, young businesses, and the work ute are in the carousel.
